title: Discover, prioritise and write stories your team can build

say: Discover, prioritise, and write stories your team can build.
This is the video for module two of Product Management Foundations.
Every product idea is a bundle of beliefs. Discovery makes those beliefs visible and tests the most dangerous ones first.

panel.heading: Three jobs in one working cycle
items: Find and test the riskiest assumptions
Choose what to build, and explain why
Write work so the team builds it right

say: Then you will have more good ideas than time, so you must choose what to do now, with reasoning people can see.

panel.heading: Three jobs in one working cycle
items: Find and test the riskiest assumptions
Choose what to build, and explain why

say: Finally, you write the chosen work so clearly that the team builds the right thing, including what happens when things go wrong.

items: Find and test the riskiest assumptions

say: Step one. Write every belief that must be true, at least 10, grouped under value, usability, feasibility and viability. For example, pharmacists reorder at least once a week.

panel.heading: Map assumptions, then test the riskiest
items: Write at least 10 beliefs that could be false
Rate each: how important, how much evidence
Pick the important ones with weak evidence
Test them in the cheapest useful way

say: Step two. Place each one on an assumption map: how important is it, and how much evidence do you already have?

panel.heading: Map assumptions, then test the riskiest
items: Write at least 10 beliefs that could be false
Rate each: how important, how much evidence
Pick the important ones with weak evidence
Test them in the cheapest useful way

say: Step three. Test the ones that are critical but have little evidence. Use an interview, a fake door test, a concierge test or a prototype, whichever is cheapest and would actually change your decision.

panel.heading: Map assumptions, then test the riskiest
items: Write at least 10 beliefs that could be false
Rate each: how important, how much evidence
Pick the important ones with weak evidence
Test them in the cheapest useful way

say: This is the rule. Critical and unproven goes first.

panel.heading: Map assumptions, then test the riskiest
items: Write at least 10 beliefs that could be false
Rate each: how important, how much evidence
Pick the important ones with weak evidence
Test them in the cheapest useful way
panel.rule: Test first: critical, with little evidence.

say: People are kind. If you ask, would you use this, most will say yes. That tells you nothing. This is the most common discovery mistake.

panel.heading: Ask about the past, not your idea
left: Would you use an app for this?
right: Tell me about the last time...

say: Instead, ask about specific past events. Tell me about the last time you ran out of stock. What did you do next? What did it cost you? Talk less and listen more, and do not pitch.

panel.heading: Ask about the past, not your idea
left: Would you use an app for this?
right: Tell me about the last time...

say: For example, Halima is exploring a stock reordering app for small pharmacies in Abuja. Her team lists 14 assumptions, and two land in the riskiest corner.

panel.heading: Halima's week of discovery

cards.d: Two land in the riskiest corner: weekly reordering, and paying a new supplier before delivery.
5 of 6 pharmacists reorder at least weekly, by phone call or WhatsApp.
Only 1 of 6 has ever paid a new supplier before delivery. The payment model must change.

say: She interviews 6 pharmacists about their last reorder. 5 of 6 reorder at least weekly. That assumption gains evidence.

panel.heading: Halima's week of discovery

cards.d: Two land in the riskiest corner: weekly reordering, and paying a new supplier before delivery.
5 of 6 pharmacists reorder at least weekly, by phone call or WhatsApp.
Only 1 of 6 has ever paid a new supplier before delivery. The payment model must change.

say: But only 1 of the 6 has ever paid a new supplier before delivery. In one week, with no code, Halima finds the payment model would likely fail, and redirects the team to pay on delivery.

panel.heading: Halima's week of discovery

cards.d: Two land in the riskiest corner: weekly reordering, and paying a new supplier before delivery.
5 of 6 pharmacists reorder at least weekly, by phone call or WhatsApp.
Only 1 of 6 has ever paid a new supplier before delivery. The payment model must change.

say: Halima's outcome is more pharmacies placing a second order within 30 days. Her team agrees four criteria: customer impact 40%, strategic fit 25%, confidence from evidence 20%, and ease of build 15%.

panel.heading: Weighted scoring, step by step
items: Pick 3 to 5 criteria from your outcome
Give weights that add to 100%
Score each option from 1 to 5
Multiply, add, and treat small gaps as ties

say: They score each option from 1 to 5. Engineers own the ease scores.

panel.heading: Weighted scoring, step by step
items: Pick 3 to 5 criteria from your outcome
Give weights that add to 100%
Score each option from 1 to 5
Multiply, add, and treat small gaps as ties

say: Pay on delivery scores 4.10. One-tap reorder scores 4.05. Loyalty points score 2.40. A gap of 0.05 is a tie, so Halima checks what users expect: paying on delivery is a must-have for most pharmacists.

panel.heading: Weighted scoring, step by step
items: Pick 3 to 5 criteria from your outcome
Give weights that add to 100%
Score each option from 1 to 5
Multiply, add, and treat small gaps as ties

say: Agree the criteria first, so nobody tunes the numbers to favour a pet idea. Then label the release: Must, pay on delivery. Should, one-tap reorder. Won't this time, loyalty points.

panel.heading: Weighted scoring, step by step
items: Pick 3 to 5 criteria from your outcome
Give weights that add to 100%
Score each option from 1 to 5
Multiply, add, and treat small gaps as ties
panel.rule: Agree criteria and weights before anyone scores.

say: Now write the work. As a pharmacist placing an order, I want to choose pay on delivery, so that I only pay once the stock is in my hands. The benefit tells the team why it matters.

panel.heading: Write a story the team can build
items: As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Check it with INVEST
Given, When, Then criteria
Cover the failure paths too

say: Check it with INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable.

panel.heading: Write a story the team can build
items: As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Check it with INVEST
Given, When, Then criteria
Cover the failure paths too

say: Then write acceptance criteria. Given an order above the limit, when the pharmacist selects pay on delivery, then the app explains the limit and offers to split the order or pay now.

panel.heading: Write a story the team can build
items: As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Check it with INVEST
Given, When, Then criteria
Cover the failure paths too

say: Cover the normal path and the important failure paths. A third criterion promises an SMS receipt within one minute of payment.

panel.heading: Write a story the team can build
items: As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Check it with INVEST
Given, When, Then criteria
Cover the failure paths too

say: When you slice a big feature into small stories, release the thinnest journey that works end to end.
But never cut the criteria that protect money or personal data to make a story smaller.
Payment confirmation, limits, receipts and access control stay in. Slice features, not safeguards.

panel.heading: Slice features, never safeguards
items: Payment confirmation
Limits
Receipts
Access control

say: To remember. Test the important, unproven assumptions first. Ask about past behaviour, not opinions. Agree criteria before scoring. Write stories with a real user and a benefit. And write criteria that cover failure, without slicing away safeguards.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Test important, unproven assumptions first
Ask about past behaviour, not opinions
Agree criteria before scoring
Stories name user, capability and benefit
Criteria cover failure paths; keep safeguards

say: Now practise. Map your assumptions and interview two people. Prioritise five features with a scoring table. Then write three delivery-ready stories with their criteria.
Save each one for your capstone, and continue with the lessons below.

panel.heading: Your practice tasks
items: Map and test one risky assumption
Prioritise five features
Write three delivery-ready stories
